topics: 🕳️ Cisterns, Dovecotes, and Trees — what's fit for the altar, what's fit for Temple maintenance, and what's fit for neither
🌱 Already There vs. Grown Afterward — Rabbi Yosei's dissent on new growth in consecrated property
🐄 No Suckling, No Snacking — why an unconsecrated calf can't nurse from a consecrated mother, and why laborers can't eat the Temple's figs
🌊 Roots, Springs, and the Golden Jug — new mishna on boundary-crossing consecrated property
💧 Reish Lakish vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan — is there a fixed measure for the water libation?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Where Consecration Does and Doesn't Reach
overview.subtitle: Meilah 13a–13b
overview.hebrewSource: וְלַד הַמְעוּשֶּׂרֶת – לֹא יִנַק מִן הַמְעוּשֶּׂרֶת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through cases where consecration's reach is ambiguous: a cistern, dovecote, or tree consecrated together with its contents is fully subject to me'ilah, but the Rabbis hold that content added AFTER consecration is not — only Rabbi Yosei disagrees for natural growth. The Gemara then derives, through verbal analogies to the firstborn offering, why an unconsecrated calf may not nurse from its now-consecrated or now-tithed mother, and why laborers and animals working with Temple produce may not eat from it. A new mishna maps consecration across physical boundaries — tree roots, spring water, and the golden jug used for the Sukkot water libation — setting up a dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan about whether that libation has a fixed measure.

slides.title: 🕳️ Fit for the Altar? Fit for Temple Maintenance? Neither?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's categories for consecrated property, and what happened AFTER consecration
rows: Cistern full of water (at consecration)
Temple maintenance only (kneading clay)
Me'ilah applies to both the cistern and the water inside
Dovecote full of pigeons / tree full of fruit (at consecration)
The altar (pigeons, fruit-wine), not maintenance
Me'ilah applies to both
Garbage dump full of manure (at consecration)
Neither altar nor maintenance
Sold; proceeds go to the Temple; me'ilah still applies to both
Empty cistern/dovecote/tree/field, filled AFTERWARD
Same categories as above
Me'ilah applies only to the vessel/land itself — NOT to what filled it later

callout.label: Rabbi Yosei's dissent:
callout.text: For a field or tree, Rabbi Yosei holds that even growth appearing AFTER consecration (grass, new fruit) IS subject to me'ilah, since it is still 'growth of consecrated property' — the Rabbis disagree only for growth, not for animals born into a pen or objects deposited afterward.

slides.title: 🐄 Why the Milk Is Off-Limits Too
slides.subtitle: Two verbal analogies (gezeirah shava) extend me'ilah to a mother's milk

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: an unconsecrated calf born to a tithed mother, or to a not-yet-consecrated sacrificial mother, may not nurse from her once she becomes tithed/consecrated

2️⃣ Source for the tithed animal's milk: the word 'passing' (הַעֲבָרָה) links tithing to the firstborn offering — just as the firstborn is subject to me'ilah in its entirety (it's male, no milk), so is the tithed animal's milk

3️⃣ Source for the sacrificial animal's milk: the word 'its mother' (אִמּוֹ) links a newborn sacrificial animal's seven days with its mother to the same phrase for a firstborn — again extending full me'ilah, including the milk
4️⃣ Result: since the milk itself is under me'ilah, allowing the unconsecrated offspring to nurse would mean it derives forbidden benefit — so it may not

callout.label: Same logic protects the Temple's produce:
callout.text: A laborer may not eat consecrated dried figs while working (derived from 'your neighbor's vineyard' — not the Temple's), and a threshing cow may not eat consecrated vetch (from 'do not muzzle an ox... in its treading' — 'its' excludes a consecrated field).

slides.title: 🐄 Two Sources, One Principle: The Temple's Produce Isn't Yours to Eat
slides.subtitle: Why the Gemara needs a separate verse for the cow but not the laborer

boxes.title: The Laborer
items: Verse: 'when you come into your neighbor's vineyard' (Deut. 23:25)
Excludes Temple property automatically — no separate derivation needed

boxes.title: The Threshing Cow
items: Verse: 'do not muzzle an ox during ITS treading' (Deut. 25:4)
'Its' (your own) treading excludes a consecrated field — you must muzzle the ox there
A separate, less obvious derivation was needed

callout.label: A further case:
callout.text: Threshing ordinary legumes (kalilin) atop a consecrated field is itself me'ilah — Ravina infers that the field's loosened dust benefits the threshing, so one derives benefit from something 'detached,' satisfying the usual requirement for misuse.

slides.title: 🌊 New Mishna: Consecration Across a Boundary
slides.subtitle: Roots, springs, the golden jug, and the willow branches
rows: Ordinary tree's roots entering consecrated land, or vice versa
No benefit ab initio; no me'ilah if benefited
Spring flowing from ordinary land INTO a consecrated field
No benefit ab initio while inside the field; no me'ilah if benefited
Once it flows back OUT: benefit is fully permitted
Water in the golden jug (drawn for the Sukkot libation, not yet in a service vessel)
No benefit ab initio; no me'ilah if benefited
Once poured into the service-vessel flask: fully subject to me'ilah
Willow branches (aravah) for the altar
No benefit ab initio; no me'ilah if benefited
Once placed at the altar (mitzva fulfilled): benefit is fully permitted — R' Elazar b. R' Tzadok: the elders even took branches for their lulav beforehand

slides.title: 💧 Is There a Fixed Measure for the Water Libation?
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree about the golden jug's flask

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: Once the water is placed in the service-vessel flask, me'ilah applies ONLY to the required three log (like the wine libation) — any water beyond that measure is not consecrated at all.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Me'ilah applies to ALL the water in the flask, however much it holds — there is no fixed maximum measure for the water libation.

lines.speaker: Challenge to Reish Lakish
lines.text: But Rabbi Elazar teaches that pouring the water libation outside the Temple courtyard carries karet, just like an ordinary offering sacrificed outside — following Rabbi Akiva's reading that 'their libations' (Num. 29:31) includes BOTH water and wine libations equally.

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Reish Lakish himself agrees there IS a fixed measure for the water (matching wine's three log) — his earlier statement about 'no measure' was framed only within Rabbi Menaḥem Yodafa's explanation of Rabbi Elazar's position, not his own view.

summary.principle: Me'ilah reaches whatever was present at the moment of consecration — and, through verbal analogies, whatever is inseparable from a consecrated body like its milk — but does not automatically extend to later growth, later arrivals, or property across a physical boundary until it truly enters the consecrated space or vessel.

flowSteps.content: 🕳️ Consecrated at the time: me'ilah applies to contents too; filled afterward: me'ilah applies only to the vessel/land
🐄 Verbal analogies to the firstborn offering extend me'ilah to a tithed/consecrated mother's milk

columns.content: 🌊 Roots, spring water, jug water: no me'ilah until truly inside consecrated space/vessel
💧 Golden jug's flask: me'ilah for three log, or for all of it — resolved in Reish Lakish's favor for a fixed measure

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: consecration's boundaries are precise — timing, physical location, and vessel-status all determine exactly what is, and isn't, subject to me'ilah

quiz.q: According to the mishna, if one consecrates an empty cistern and it is later filled with water, what is the halakha?
o: Me'ilah applies to both the cistern and the water
Me'ilah applies only to the cistern, not to the water that filled it afterward
Me'ilah applies only to the water, not the cistern
Neither the cistern nor the water is subject to me'ilah
quiz.e: The mishna distinguishes items present at the time of consecration (fully subject to me'ilah) from items that arrive afterward (only the original vessel/land remains subject to me'ilah).

quiz.q: How does the Gemara derive that the milk of a sacrificial animal's mother is prohibited to her not-yet-consecrated offspring?
o: From a direct verse stating this explicitly
Through a verbal analogy ('its mother') linking the sacrificial animal to the firstborn offering, which is subject to me'ilah in its entirety
From the laws governing tithed produce only
There is no derivation; it is a rabbinic decree with no source
quiz.e: The Gemara uses the shared phrase 'its mother' between the sacrificial animal verse and the firstborn offering verse to extend full me'ilah — including the milk — to the sacrificial mother.

quiz.q: Why does a threshing cow need a separate verse to be excluded from eating consecrated vetch, while a laborer needs no separate derivation to be excluded from eating consecrated figs?
o: Because cows have no legal status in Jewish law
Because the laborer's verse ('your neighbor's vineyard') naturally excludes Temple property, while the cow's exclusion requires the specific phrase 'its treading' from 'do not muzzle an ox'
Because consecrated produce is never edible by animals
Because the mishna does not actually discuss the cow's case
quiz.e: The laborer's exclusion follows automatically from the wording 'your neighbor's,' but the ox-muzzling verse needed the added word 'its' to specifically exclude a consecrated field from the general rule.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, when does one become liable for misusing water drawn for the Sukkot water libation in the golden jug?
o: From the moment it is drawn from the Siloam pool
Only once it is poured into the service-vessel flask
It is never subject to me'ilah
Only after the libation is poured on the altar
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that the water in the golden jug (not yet a service vessel) carries no me'ilah liability; only once transferred into the flask, a consecrated service vessel, does me'ilah apply.

quiz.q: How is the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan about the water libation's measure ultimately resolved?
o: Rabbi Yoḥanan is proven correct with no further discussion

Reish Lakish's apparent inconsistency is resolved: he does hold there is a fixed measure of three log, matching wine; his 'no measure' statement was only describing Rabbi Menaḥem Yodafa's explanation of Rabbi Elazar's view, not his own position
The Gemara declares the question unresolved (teiku)
Both agree there is no measure for water at all
quiz.e: The Gemara clarifies that Reish Lakish's own view holds there IS a fixed three-log measure for the water libation, paralleling wine; his earlier statement was made only in the context of explaining someone else's position.
